title: Financial Modelling in Spreadsheets
summary: Learn to build clear, reliable financial models: structure and good practice, PMT, NPV and IRR, revenue and cost forecasts, linking the three statements, scenarios and sensitivity, and checking and presenting results.
audience: Finance and accounting students, analysts, entrepreneurs and managers who use spreadsheets

body.p: A financial model is a spreadsheet that represents a business or project in numbers so you can forecast results, test decisions and raise money. Good models are clear, accurate and easy for someone else to check.

list: Inputs (assumptions): growth rates, prices, costs, interest rates, all in one clearly labelled place.
Calculations: formulas that use the inputs, never typed-in numbers.
Outputs: summaries, financial statements, charts and key ratios.
Checks: formulas that confirm the model balances and flag errors.
Colour-code cells, for example blue for inputs and black for formulas.
Keep one formula consistent across a row; avoid one-off changes in the middle.
Show units and time periods in labels ("R'000, monthly").
Never hard-code a number inside a formula, such as =B5*1.15; put 15% in an input cell and refer to it.
Keep formulas short; split long ones into steps.

body.tip: Before building, sketch on paper what questions the model must answer; it keeps the model focused.

body.p: Money now is worth more than the same amount later, because it can earn a return. Spreadsheets have built-in functions for these calculations; the examples below were checked independently in code.

A loan of R100 000 at 12% a year, repaid monthly over 36 months, uses a monthly rate of 1%. =PMT(1%, 36, -100000) gives about R3321.43 a month. Total repaid is about R119 571, so total interest is about R19 571.52.

A project costs R100 000 now and returns R30 000 a year for 5 years. At a 10% discount rate, the net present value is -100 000 + NPV(10%, five years of 30 000), about R13 724. A positive NPV means the project earns more than 10%. Its internal rate of return, the rate where NPV is zero, is about 15.24%. At 12% the NPV falls to about R8143.

list: In Excel and Google Sheets, NPV discounts from the first cash flow listed, so add the time-zero investment separately.
IRR can mislead when cash flows change sign several times or projects differ greatly in size; prefer NPV for decisions.
XNPV and XIRR handle irregular dates.

body.tip: Always state whether rates are annual or monthly, and match them to the period of the cash flows.

body.p: Forecasts turn assumptions into numbers. Build revenue from its drivers rather than guessing a total: customers x purchases per customer x average price, or units x price.

Revenue of R500 000 growing 8% a year becomes R540 000, R583 200 and R629 856 over the next three years. In the spreadsheet, each year's formula is the previous year times (1 + the growth input), so changing one input updates every year.

list: Variable costs as a percentage of revenue or per unit: cost of sales, commissions, delivery.
Fixed costs as amounts that change in steps: rent, salaries (with hiring plans), insurance.
Capital expenditure and depreciation for equipment and buildings.
Working capital: debtor days, stock days and creditor days, which drive cash tied up in the business.

body.p: Example: monthly revenue of R120 000 with a 35% gross margin gives R42 000 gross profit; after R30 000 of fixed overheads, operating profit is R12 000.

body.tip: Compare forecasts with history and industry benchmarks; growth far above either needs a strong explanation.

body.p: Full models link the income statement, balance sheet and cash-flow statement so they stay consistent.

list: Profit after tax from the income statement flows to retained earnings on the balance sheet and starts the cash-flow statement.
Non-cash items such as depreciation are added back in the cash-flow statement.
Changes in debtors, stock and creditors adjust profit to cash: more debtors means less cash.
Capital expenditure appears in investing cash flows and increases fixed assets; depreciation reduces them.
Loans raised or repaid appear in financing cash flows and change debt on the balance sheet.
Closing cash from the cash-flow statement becomes the cash line on the balance sheet.

body.p: Assets must equal liabilities plus equity in every period. Build a check row (assets minus liabilities minus equity) that should show zero, and highlight any non-zero result. If it does not balance, trace the first period where it breaks.

body.tip: Profitable businesses can still run out of cash. Always look at the cash forecast, not just profit.

body.p: Forecasts are uncertain, so good models show how results change when assumptions change.

list: Sensitivity analysis changes one input at a time. If yearly returns are R25 000 instead of R30 000, the project's NPV at 10% falls from about R13 724 to about -R5230, so the decision is very sensitive to that assumption.
Data tables in spreadsheets calculate an output for a grid of input values, such as NPV for several discount rates and growth rates.
Scenario analysis changes several inputs together: base, best and worst cases, selected with a switch cell.
Break-even or goal-seek finds the input value that makes an output hit a target, for example the price that gives NPV of zero.

body.p: Present ranges and the key drivers rather than a single number. Decision-makers need to know which assumptions matter most, so they can test them or manage the risk.

body.tip: Spend most of your checking effort on the two or three inputs that move the answer most.

body.p: Spreadsheet errors are common and can be costly. Build in checks and review models systematically.

list: Use check cells: balance sheet balances, cash never negative without a loan, totals agree.
Trace precedents and dependents to see what a formula uses and what uses it.
Look for hard-coded numbers, broken ranges and inconsistent formulas across rows.
Test with simple inputs where you know the answer, such as zero growth.
Ask someone else to review; fresh eyes catch errors.
Keep version control: save dated versions and record changes.

body.p: Put a short summary sheet first: key outputs, the main assumptions and a chart or two. Label units clearly, round sensibly for presentation and explain limitations. Protect formula cells to prevent accidental changes, leaving inputs editable.

body.tip: If a number in a presentation surprises you, find out why before anyone else asks.
